notEncrypted.reinstall: This device is not encrypted, and its agent reports no disk layout that can be encrypted in place. Encrypt it by reinstalling it with the Paddock autoinstall after a backup.

unmanaged.reinstall: This device was encrypted outside Paddock: no recovery key or header is escrowed, and a Lock cannot be restored. Reinstall it with the Paddock autoinstall to manage its encryption.

convert.label: Encrypt this device…
convert.eligible: This device is not encrypted. Its disk layout allows encrypting it in place: the device prepares itself, the recovery key is stored in Paddock first, the user restarts once to start the encryption, the rest is encrypted in the background, and the boot PIN or the TPM unlock is set up at the first restart after that.
convert.title: Encrypt {hostname} in place
convert.explanation: Paddock encrypts the root partition of this device without reinstalling it. Nothing changes until the device restarts; the recovery key is stored in Paddock before the first byte is encrypted. Data outside the root partition (other partitions, swap partitions) is not encrypted.

check.backup: I confirm that a current backup of this device exists. The file system is checked and shrunk at the restart, which can take several minutes; a power cut or a forced power-off during that time can damage it.
check.restart: The user must restart the device once to start the encryption, and once more after it has completed. Nothing is encrypted until the first restart, which takes a few minutes longer than usual.
check.power: A laptop must be on mains power at that restart; the background encryption pauses on battery.
check.pin: At the first restart after the background encryption has completed, the device asks the user for a boot PIN on a text console (unlock mode: TPM + boot PIN). The PIN never reaches Paddock.
check.tpmOnly: The device sets up its TPM unlock without a PIN at the first restart after the background encryption has completed (unlock mode: TPM only).
check.duration: The background encryption takes about {duration} on this disk; the device stays usable meanwhile.
check.durationUnknown: The background encryption takes minutes to hours depending on the disk size; the device stays usable meanwhile.
check.initramfsSwitch: The device switches its early-boot system from initramfs-tools to dracut. revocation.title: Lock and Destroy

Encrypted volumes without an escrowed header are not erased by a Lock. openbao.title: OpenBao
openbao.summary: OpenBao holds every key of this installation. It starts sealed after every restart; three custodians unseal it, or, if you accept the risk below, the unsealer on the control-plane host does.

setting.title: Automatic unseal
setting.outdated: The disclaimer has changed since this acknowledgement.

openbao.disableConfirmMessage: Automatic unseal stops at once. The shares stay on the host until an operator runs ./paddock auto-unseal disable.

disclaimer.title: Enable automatic unseal of OpenBao
disclaimer.intro: Automatic unseal keeps three of the five unseal shares on the control-plane host, in .secrets/openbao/auto-unseal-shares. A small service on that host, the unsealer, reads them and unseals OpenBao whenever it starts sealed, as long as this setting is on.
disclaimer.lead: Before you enable it, understand and accept these consequences:
disclaimer.risk1: Whoever controls the host controls every key. Anyone with root on the host, a copy of its disk, a snapshot of the virtual machine or a copy of .secrets/ can unseal OpenBao and use every key in it: the signing keys for device configuration, commands and revocation tokens, the escrow key that decrypts the escrowed disk recovery material of every device, the audit chain key and the portal session keys.
disclaimer.risk2: The custodian model no longer protects the unseal. Today three named custodians must act together before OpenBao unseals. With automatic unseal their shares still exist, but three of them lie on the host; no person has to act, and no one is asked.
disclaimer.risk3: Copies and backups of the host become as sensitive as the keys. Paddock never writes the shares into its own backups, but a disk image, a VM snapshot or a copy of the bundle directory does contain them, and nothing in Paddock can tell that such a copy exists.
disclaimer.risk4: This is a residual risk of your information security management system (RR-43 in docs/compliance/residual-risks.md). Record it with an owner and a decision. On a production host, ./paddock check warns on every run while automatic unseal is on.
disclaimer.outro: Enabling here places no share on the host. It records your acknowledgement, with your name, the time and the version of this text ({version}), in the audit log. An operator with access to the host then runs ./paddock auto-unseal enable, which refuses to run without this acknowledgement. Disabling here stops the automatic unseal at once; the shares stay on the host until the operator runs ./paddock auto-unseal disable.
disclaimer.sentence: I understand and accept the risk
